sections.heading: Stories from the ground
sections.lead: What the numbers look like when they happen to one group.

sections.body: Stories are published with the written consent of the group and the individuals named. Where consent is limited, names and locations are changed and we say so. **Replace the illustrative examples below with your verified stories before publication.**

sections.note: The three stories below are ILLUSTRATIVE EXAMPLES from the design template, not verified CECF beneficiary accounts — see media/photos/PLACEHOLDERS.md. Do not seed these as real testimonials without written consent per the note above.

items.title: “The bank had refused us twice. It was the same bank.”
body: A women’s group in Kamukunji had been saving for four years, held KES 240,000 between them, and had been turned away twice — not for lack of money, but because there was no group to lend to. The savings sat in the treasurer’s personal M-Pesa.
Registration took nine weeks. The account opened three weeks after that. The third application, to the same branch, was approved.
items.quote: What changed was not our money. It was that we finally existed on their paper.

photo.alt: A woman selling carrots at a Kenyan market

items.title: A dispute that would have ended a fourteen-year chama
body: Two office-bearers disagreed over a withdrawal. Within a month the group had split into factions and stopped meeting. Fourteen years of savings were sitting untouched because nobody could agree who had authority to move them.

A community mediator trained through the Judiciary programme — herself a member of a neighbouring group — brought both sides to a settlement in two sessions. The group has since registered and reopened contributions.

photo.alt: A trader selling bananas at a market in Kenya

items.title: “We could finally show a buyer a transaction history.”
body: A hardware traders’ cooperative had supplied the same customers for six years on trust and handwritten receipts. A county tender required a compliant invoice and a bank reference neither existed.
Registration, a KRA PIN and eTIMS onboarding took under three months. The cooperative’s first tender bid, aggregated with two other groups through the digital platform, was successful.
